title: Thu phí ùn tắc · Problems / Solutions
prompt: Some societies are considering charging drivers to enter congested city centres. What problems could this create, and what measures could be taken to address them?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: Congestion charges make drivers confront the cost of occupying scarce city-centre road space. Charges can burden essential travellers who lack alternatives, requiring better service coverage and narrowly targeted exemptions rather than identical treatment of every journey.

People working unsocial hours may have no realistic alternative to driving. Travellers with fixed hours and no suitable public service cannot easily change their route or departure time. They may continue driving and absorb the charge, so the policy's financial burden can fall on essential journeys rather than only discourage flexible or unnecessary traffic. A commuter served by frequent trains can respond to the charge differently from a night-shift worker whose bus route stops operating before work ends. A hospital worker finishing after midnight cannot necessarily switch to a train designed around daytime demand, even if the station is close to the workplace. Repeated charges then reduce disposable income without reducing the number of essential journeys, making an apparently neutral price particularly burdensome for workers with rigid schedules.

Revenue should improve transport coverage and provide narrowly defined exemptions. Better coverage expands alternatives, while narrowly defined exemptions recognise necessity without allowing so many free entries that congestion simply returns. Authorities should map early and late shifts against service timetables before setting exemptions, because a bus route on a map is not an alternative if its last departure precedes the worker's shift. Extending service hours can create a real alternative for these passengers; until that is available, carefully verified exemptions should recognise necessary travel rather than reward anyone who merely prefers driving.
Overall, success should combine reduced congestion with usable alternatives for essential journeys, rather than assume that every fall in car entries represents an equitable outcome.

paragraphs.quote: Revenue should improve transport coverage and provide narrowly defined exemptions. Better coverage expands alternatives, while narrowly defined exemptions recognise necessity without allowing so many free entries that congestion simply returns. Authorities should map early and late shifts against service timetables before setting exemptions, because a bus route on a map is not an alternative if its last departure precedes the worker's shift. Extending service hours can create a real alternative for these passengers; until that is available, carefully verified exemptions should recognise necessary travel rather than reward anyone who merely prefers driving.
